lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Careers in Science and How They Improve Human Life

pages.body:
Think about everything you used or saw since you woke up. The water from the tap, the medicine in the clinic, the phone on the table, the food in the market and the road to school all depend on science and the people who work in it.

- Which people make sure that these things work and are safe?
- What would you like to be when you grow up? What science would you need to learn for it?

Science is not only a school subject. It is the basis of many careers that improve how people live. In this lesson we study a range of science careers, see how each one helps humans and think about the careers that Ghana most needs.

We begin with what scientists and technologists do for society.

pages.title: Why careers in science matter
pages.body:
Scientists ask questions about the natural world and test their answers. Technologists and engineers use this knowledge to design tools, medicines, machines and systems that solve problems. Together, their work improves health, food supply, safety, communication, transport and care of the environment.

Next we look at the work of people in different fields.

pages.title: Some careers in science and technology
pages.body:
| **Career** | **What the person does** | **How it improves human life** |
|---|---|---|
| Medical doctor and nurse | Diagnose illness and care for patients | Cure disease and save lives |
| Pharmacist | Prepares and gives medicines and advises on their use | Makes sure that medicines are safe and correct |
| Medical laboratory scientist | Tests blood and other samples | Helps doctors find the cause of disease |
| Agricultural scientist and extension officer | Study crops, soils and animals and teach farmers | Increase food production and protect farmers' income |
| Veterinarian | Treats and protects the health of animals | Keeps livestock healthy and prevents animal diseases from spreading to people |
| Food scientist | Studies how to process, preserve and improve food | Reduces food waste and improves nutrition |
| Engineer | Designs and builds structures, machines and power systems | Provides roads, buildings, electricity and water |
| Environmental scientist | Studies pollution, climate and waste | Protects air, water and soil |
| Geologist and mining engineer | Study rocks and minerals and extract them | Provide gold, bauxite, oil and building materials |
| Meteorologist | Studies and forecasts weather | Warns farmers and communities about rain, floods and storms |
| Computer scientist and software developer | Design computer programs and networks | Make communication, banking and learning faster |
| Science teacher | Teaches science and guides learners | Prepares the next generation of scientists |
| Astronomer and physicist | Study the Sun, planets, matter and energy | Expand our understanding of the universe and lead to new technologies |

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Science, technology and innovation in everyday life

pages.body:
Now we see how science and technology appear in homes, schools, communities and the universe.

## Science, technology and innovation in everyday life

- In homes. Refrigerators keep food from spoiling, cookers and LED lamps use energy more efficiently, and mobile phones connect families.
- In schools. Computers, projectors and science laboratories help learners study, and filters make drinking water safe.
- In communities. Clinics, boreholes, bridges, mobile money services and solar street lights improve daily life.
- In the universe. Telescopes and satellites let us study the planets and stars, forecast the weather and find our way with navigation systems. In 2017 the GhanaSat 1 satellite, built by university students in Ghana, was put into orbit and shows that young Ghanaians can take part in space science.
Finally we discuss which careers Ghana needs most and explain why.

lessons.title: Careers that Ghana should focus on

pages.title: Careers that Ghana should focus on
pages.body:
- Agriculture and food processing, because most Ghanaians depend on farming and processing adds value to crops and reduces waste.
- Health sciences, because a healthy population is able to learn and work.
- Renewable energy and engineering, because the country needs reliable and cleaner power.
- Information and communication technology, because it supports every other sector.
- Environmental science and climate studies, because of floods, waste, deforestation and climate change.
- Mining, oil and gas engineering, to manage natural resources responsibly and add value to them.
- Science and mathematics teaching, because every other career depends on good teachers.

pages.body:
Think of someone you know who has solved a problem in your community using what they learned in science. It may be a nurse who treated a child, a farmer who improved a crop or a teacher who inspired a class.

- What kind of science did this person use?
- What do you think made this person succeed?

Behind every great discovery there is a person who asked questions, worked hard and did not give up. In this lesson we study the work of Ghanaian and international scientists and science educators and link their work to science careers.

We begin with scientists from our own country whose work is known across the world.

pages.title: Ghanaian scientists
pages.body:
- Professor Francis Allotey (1932 to 2017) was a mathematician and physicist from Saltpond. He was the first Ghanaian full professor of mathematics, working at Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology. He is known for the Allotey formalism, which arose from his work on soft X ray spectroscopy. He led the Ghana Academy of Arts and Sciences and helped found the African Physical Society. Career links. Mathematician, physicist and university lecturer.
- Professor Marian Ewurama Addy (1942 to 2014) was a biochemist at the University of Ghana. She studied the safety and effectiveness of herbal medicines and her research on the herb Desmodium adscendens helped to show its value in treating asthma. She was the first Ghanaian woman to become a full professor of natural science and the first quiz mistress of the National Science and Maths Quiz. In 1999 she won the UNESCO Kalinga Prize for the popularisation of science. Career links. Biochemist, researcher in herbal medicine and science communicator.
- Professor Ibok Oduro of Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology is a food scientist. Her research focuses on indigenous and underused African crops such as sweet potato, yam bean and breadfruit, and on turning them into foods and other products. Career links. Food scientist and researcher in post harvest technology.
Next we look at educators who have helped Ghanaian learners study science.

pages.title: Ghanaian science educators
pages.body:
- Professor Jophus Anamuah-Mensah is an expert in science education who held senior positions at the University of Cape Coast and became the first Vice Chancellor of the University of Education, Winneba. He has published many works on teaching science and in 2006 received the national honour of the Order of the Volta. Career links. Science educator, university administrator and curriculum specialist.
- Theophilus Ossei-Anto is a specialist in science and technology education who has lectured at the University of Cape Coast and has written about how science and technology should be taught in Ghana. Career links. Science educator and researcher in education.
- Professor Christian Anthony-Krueger is another science educator named in the curriculum. Your teacher may guide you to find out about his work in science education using the library or the internet.
Now we study scientists from other countries whose work has changed how we understand the world.

pages.title: International scientists
pages.body:
| **Scientist** | **Years** | **Field and main achievement** | **Career link** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Albert Einstein | 1879 to 1955 | Developed the theory of relativity and explained the photoelectric effect, for which he received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1921 | Physicist |
| Alexander Fleming | 1881 to 1955 | Discovered penicillin in 1928, the first widely used antibiotic. He shared the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1945 | Microbiologist and doctor |
| Charles Darwin | 1809 to 1882 | Proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection in On the Origin of Species, published in 1859 | Naturalist and biologist |
| Stephen Hawking | 1942 to 2018 | Made major contributions to the study of black holes and the origin of the universe and wrote the popular book A Brief History of Time | Physicist and cosmologist |

> **Note to the teacher** The curriculum list of international scientists includes the name Paul Ratnei. This name could not be matched to a known scientist, so it may be a spelling error. Learners may research another scientist of their own choice in its place.

Finally we use what we know to research the impact of science, technology and innovation and present our findings.

lessons.title: Building a portfolio and giving a presentation

pages.title: Building a portfolio and giving a presentation
pages.body:
1. Choose one theme such as health, farming, communication or space. Research how science and technology have changed that area in homes, schools, communities and the universe.
2. Collect information and pictures from books, newspapers and the internet. Always note where each piece of information came from.
3. Arrange the work in a folder under headings. Include a short biography of one scientist and a description of the career linked to that scientist.
4. Prepare a presentation of about five minutes, using a poster or slides.
5. Take questions from the class and discuss which careers Ghana should focus on.

[[pic: Timeline poster with portraits replaced by blank frames and captions. The captions give the names of Allotey, Addy, Oduro, Einstein, Fleming, Darwin and Hawking with dates and one achievement for each. Learners add drawings.]]

questions.q: Explain why a portfolio helps you to learn about the impact of science.

parts.a: It makes you research a theme, collect information and pictures from different sources, arrange it under headings and present it, so you learn how science has changed homes, schools, communities and the universe.

ideas.t: You research and collect information and pictures from different sources
You arrange and present it, learning how science has changed life

pages.body:
- Scientists study the natural world, and technologists and engineers use that knowledge to solve problems.
- Careers in science include medicine, pharmacy, agriculture, veterinary science, food science, engineering, environmental science, geology, meteorology, computing, teaching and physics.
- Science, technology and innovation improve life in homes, schools, communities and even in space exploration.
- Ghana should focus on agriculture and food processing, health, renewable energy, information technology, environmental science, mining and oil and gas, and science teaching.
- Ghanaian scientists such as Francis Allotey, Ewurama Addy and Ibok Oduro have contributed to mathematics, herbal medicine and food science.
- International scientists such as Einstein, Fleming, Darwin and Hawking changed how we understand matter, disease, life and the universe.
- A portfolio and presentation help learners to research and share what they learn about science and its impact.
